The manipulation of time in the story is exceptionally well-balanced and serves the emotional core of the narrative. The author establishes a clear timeframe for the central scene—the forty minutes it takes for the ambulance to arrive—and uses the transitions of light (from late afternoon sun, to blue light, to indigo twilight, to moonlight) to pace this period naturally. 

Within this forty-minute window, the author skillfully alternates between real-time monologue and the compression of time. Decades of Daniel’s life—his thirty-one-year marriage, his thirty-five-year career as a surveyor, the death of his dog, and his ongoing bi-weekly calls with his ex-wife—are compressed into brief, poignant paragraphs of dialogue and reflection. Similarly, the stretches of silence as he waits with the body are compressed ("He sat with her a long time without speaking") so the pacing never drags, while still making the reader feel the weight and stillness of the moment. This interplay between a short, fixed window of "story time" and the vast compression of a whole lifetime reinforces the story's central theme: that everything is on a "different clock" and life is precious because of its brevity.
